Chapter Seven: The Struggle for Stability
Life in Clarkston was anything but simple for the Fugees. Off the soccer field, these boys and their families faced a whole maze of challenges—unpredictable work hours, crowded apartments, and that constant, looming worry about eviction.
Imagine coming home after a long day, only to find out your rent’s going up and you might not be able to stay. That was the reality for so many parents—some of them juggling two, sometimes even three jobs, just to keep a roof over their heads. And while they worked, the older kids often stepped up, caring for their younger siblings.
But work wasn’t the only struggle. There were memories, too—hard ones. Things they’d left behind in other countries, shadows that showed up in nightmares or sudden moments of fear.
One evening, a boy from Liberia showed up to practice late. He looked exhausted, his face heavy with worry. His family just found out their rent was going up, and suddenly, they weren’t sure they could stay in their apartment.
The coach listened, wishing there was more she could do. Sometimes, all she could offer was a ride home, a bag of groceries, or just a promise to help however she could.
Here’s the thing—most people never see these invisible battles. For families like his, that fight for stability is never-ending, and even the smallest victories feel huge. But the Fugees? They learned to adapt. They looked out for each other. And no matter what, they still found moments to laugh and connect, even when life felt especially tough.
The coach became a lifeline for so many families. She helped them make sense of complicated paperwork, filled out forms, translated official documents, and even spoke up for kids at school. She saw firsthand just how easy it was for the system to let people slip through the cracks, and she fought hard to make sure her players didn’t get lost along the way.
Through all of this, the team became a real source of strength. Out on the field, the boys could escape their worries, even if it was just for a little while. They focused on the rhythm of the game, the thud of the ball, the simple joy of running free.
It became clear—soccer wasn’t just a game for them. It was a way to hang on to hope, even when everything else in their world felt uncertain.
